seoTitle: How to Fix Outlook/Hotmail 'Too Many Requests' Error 429
metaDescription: Fix the Hotmail or Outlook 'Too Many Requests' error 429 caused by frequent logins or refreshes with these step-by-step solutions.
intro: The Outlook or Hotmail "Too Many Requests" error 429 shows up when Microsoft's servers temporarily block your account activity because too many requests came in from your browser in a short window — usually from frequent refreshes, repeated login attempts, or a browser extension quietly hammering the login endpoint in the background. It looks alarming, but it's a rate-limit protection, not an account lockout or hack. This guide walks through the fixes in the order that actually resolves it fastest: clearing stale session data first, then isolating whether a browser extension is the real cause, before you consider anything as drastic as resetting your connection.

steps.heading: Understand what's actually happening
steps.body: Error 429 specifically means too many requests were sent to the server in too short a time, and Microsoft's servers respond by temporarily blocking further requests to protect the service rather than letting it get overwhelmed. It's most often caused by cached login data, stale cookies, or a browser extension repeatedly triggering requests behind the scenes — not by anything unusual or malicious happening on your account. Knowing this up front matters because it tells you where to look first: your browser's stored data, not your account security.

steps.heading: Clear cache and cookies for Outlook or Hotmail specifically
steps.body: Open your browser's settings and go to Privacy and Security, then Third-party cookies, then See all site data. Search for Outlook or Hotmail in that list and delete all stored data tied to those sites rather than wiping your entire browser history. This clears the old session files that are the single most common cause of a lingering 429 error, since a corrupted or outdated session token can keep triggering failed requests every time the page tries to refresh itself.

steps.heading: Disable browser extensions one at a time
steps.body: Go to your browser's Extensions section and disable extensions individually rather than all at once — ad blockers, VPNs, and password managers are the most common culprits, since they can intercept or duplicate requests to Outlook's login endpoint without you noticing. After disabling each one, check Outlook again before moving to the next; this isolates exactly which extension is causing the conflict instead of leaving you guessing after a blanket disable.

steps.heading: Test in Incognito mode or a different browser
steps.body: Open Outlook in an Incognito or Private window, which bypasses your regular cache and most extensions entirely. If Outlook loads fine there, you've confirmed the issue was cached files or an extension rather than anything wrong with your account or Microsoft's servers. You can also try a completely different browser, like Firefox or Edge, to isolate whether the problem is specific to one browser's stored data.

steps.heading: Reset your internet connection if the error persists
steps.body: If clearing data and testing in Incognito mode didn't resolve it, restart your router or switch to a different network. Repeated requests routed through the same IP address can sometimes keep the rate limit active even after your browser-side data is clean, particularly if multiple devices on the same network have been hitting Outlook around the same time.

steps.heading: Avoid the patterns that trigger it again
steps.body: Once you're back in, avoid rapid repeated refreshing or logging in and out in quick succession, since this is the most common way the rate limit gets triggered in the first place. If you regularly use Outlook across several devices, stagger your logins rather than opening the same account everywhere at once — simultaneous activity from multiple sessions is one of the patterns Microsoft's rate limiting is specifically designed to catch.

faq.question: How long does the 429 error usually last?
faq.answer: It's typically temporary and can clear within minutes to a few hours, depending on how the rate limit was triggered.

faq.question: Does this error mean my account was hacked?
faq.answer: Not necessarily — it's more often related to activity patterns like frequent refreshes or a misbehaving browser extension rather than a security breach.

faq.question: Can using multiple devices at once cause this error?
faq.answer: Yes, logging in and refreshing from several devices simultaneously can contribute to triggering the rate limit.

faq.question: Will clearing my cache delete my emails?
faq.answer: No, clearing your browser's cached data and cookies doesn't delete emails, which remain stored safely on Microsoft's servers.

faq.question: How do I tell if a browser extension is causing the error?
faq.answer: Open Outlook in Incognito or Private mode, which disables most extensions by default. If the error disappears there, re-enable your extensions one at a time in normal mode, checking Outlook after each one, until you find the culprit.
